learningModules.title: Module 1: What We Measured vs. What We're Modeling
learningModules.description: A direct accounting of what a public scan of your pricing page can and can't tell us, and how to close the gap with your own data.
learningModules.content:
What we measured directly from your pricing page's HTML: 5 plan tiers, an average of ~22 feature bullet points per plan (~110 discrete data points total), a 3.4s mobile LCP, and no usage-based savings calculator anywhere on the page. Those are facts about the page, not about your users.

What we don't have: your actual visitor count, session duration, or conversion rate on that page. Those live in your analytics stack, which we have no access to. Any specific dollar figure for 'lost revenue' would have to invent a traffic number and a conversion rate — we're not going to do that.

What the measured facts support is a well-documented pattern: 5 plans × 22 features is an expert-level cognitive task for a first-time visitor, and for a payments product specifically, uncertainty about which plan is correct compounds with the perceived risk of misconfiguring live transaction infrastructure. Whether that pattern is actually suppressing your conversion rate — and by how much — is something only your own analytics can confirm.

How to check: pull your pricing_page_loaded → checkout_initiated conversion rate from your existing analytics before changing anything. That single number is worth more than anything in this document.

learningModules.title: Module 2: The Savings-First Page Architecture
learningModules.description: Restructure the pricing page to anchor value before revealing cost — the change we'd recommend testing first, grounded in what we measured.
learningModules.content:
The insight: when a user sees an estimated annual savings figure before they see your subscription price, the subscription cost reads as a return, not an expense. Ordering of information matters as much as the information itself.

New page structure (top to bottom):
1. Headline: 'How much are you paying in payment fees right now?' — interactive input field
2. Savings calculator: user enters their own monthly transaction volume; the calculator outputs their estimated current processor cost versus PayFlux, with the annual delta in large, bold typography
3. Plan recommendation: one plan, pre-selected based on their input — not a five-way grid
4. Plan details: the 5 key features of the recommended plan only, with a progressive toggle to see the full comparison
5. CTA: trial or checkout, framed against the number they just saw

This does three things at once: quantifies value in the user's own numbers, removes the self-classification burden by recommending a plan, and positions the subscription cost as a fraction of the savings it implies.

Implementation estimate: redesign + copywriting + calculator logic, roughly 5–8 engineering days. We can't promise a specific conversion outcome — see Module 1 on why — but this is the highest-leverage structural change available given what we measured.

learningModules.title: Module 3: Building the Savings Calculator Without Overclaiming
learningModules.description: The calculator logic, and the guardrails needed so the numbers it shows are ones you can actually stand behind.
learningModules.content:
Calculator logic:

Inputs: monthly transaction volume ($) + average transaction value ($)
Competitor cost estimate: use a documented, current published rate for whichever processor you're comparing against — do not use a stale or rounded figure, it will be checked by sophisticated buyers
PayFlux cost: apply your actual rate card at the estimated volume tier
Savings delta: competitor estimate − PayFlux cost

Display format example: 'At $50,000/month in transactions, you'd pay an estimated $X/month with [competitor]. PayFlux costs $99/month — a modeled savings of $Y/month.' Label it modeled, not guaranteed, since actual fees depend on account-specific factors you don't control.

Design notes:
— Default the calculator to whatever volume figure matches your actual median customer, once you know it from your own data — we don't have that number
— Update the recommended plan in real time as the input changes
— Route volumes above your top tier to an inline Enterprise contact form, not a separate page

Edge case: at low volumes, the savings delta may be small or negative. Don't hide this — show the plan's non-cost value drivers (fraud protection, instant payouts, reconciliation) instead of forcing a savings narrative that doesn't hold.

learningModules.title: Module 4: Pricing Page Telemetry — What to Measure and When
learningModules.description: The PostHog events that would give you complete visibility into pricing page behavior and let you attribute any conversion change to a specific cause.
learningModules.content:
Deploy in priority order:

1. posthog.capture('pricing_page_loaded', { referrer, utm_source }) — baseline + traffic source
2. posthog.capture('calculator_interacted', { volume_input, avg_transaction_input, recommended_plan }) — measures savings calculator adoption, once shipped
3. posthog.capture('plan_recommended', { plan, monthly_savings }) — tracks which plans the calculator recommends most
4. posthog.capture('checkout_initiated', { plan, volume_estimate }) — the conversion event
5. posthog.capture('pricing_abandoned', { time_on_page, calculator_used }) — exit intent with calculator engagement flag

Run these for at least 2 weeks before the redesign to get a real baseline, and 2 weeks after to measure the actual delta — this is what turns the modeled 10–25% range into a number you can trust. Weekly review focus once live: the calculator_used flag on abandoned sessions — users who interact with the calculator but still leave are hitting a different friction point, worth investigating separately.

diagnosis.signal: PayFlux's pricing page displays 5 plan tiers with an average of ~22 feature bullet points each — ~110 discrete data points, measured directly from the page's HTML. The page also has no usage-based savings calculator and a 3.4s mobile LCP. We do not have your visitor count, session duration, or conversion rate — those require your own analytics, which we don't have access to. What we can say is that a page asking a first-time visitor to self-classify across 110 data points is a documented friction pattern; whether it's actually suppressing your conversion rate is something only your own funnel data can confirm.

friction.mechanism: Pricing Paralysis via Feature Overload (measured structure, modeled behavioral impact)
friction.rootCause: 5 plans × ~22 feature line-items require a first-time visitor to process ~110 discrete data points before selecting a plan. For a payments infrastructure product specifically, the cognitive overhead of self-classifying into the correct tier compounds with the perceived risk of misconfiguring live transaction infrastructure — a documented pattern in checkout-usability research, not something we've measured on your actual users.

finalDecision.label: Collapse to 3 plans with 5 features each
finalDecision.action: Reduce visible plans from 5 to 3 (Starter, Growth, Scale) after confirming usage distribution with your own data. Display only 5 key differentiating features per plan. Gate Enterprise behind an inline contact form. Add a progressive-disclosure toggle for the full feature list.
finalDecision.reasoning: Of the three approaches, this is the one most directly grounded in what we actually measured — plan count and feature density — without requiring you to build new calculator infrastructure before you've validated the simpler fix. It's also the easiest to reverse if it underperforms.
finalDecision.tradeoff: Requires you to check plan-usage data first (see Avoid section) — skipping that check risks archiving a plan your best customers rely on. Some enterprise-tier prospects may feel constrained by the reduced default feature set; the progressive-disclosure toggle mitigates this.

decisions.label: Collapse to 3 plans with 5 features each
decisions.action: Reduce visible plans from 5 to 3 (Starter, Growth, Scale). Display only 5 key differentiating features per plan. Archive Micro as a legacy tier only after confirming its usage. Gate Enterprise behind an inline contact form.
decisions.reasoning: Hick's Law predicts decision time increases with option count — cutting from 5 to 3 plans and 22 to 5 features directly reduces the measured complexity. Published checkout research associates this pattern with meaningfully higher checkout initiation, though that's a benchmark, not a measurement of PayFlux specifically.
decisions.tradeoff: Some enterprise-tier prospects may feel constrained by the reduced visible feature set. The progressive disclosure toggle addresses this without cluttering the default view.

decisions.label: Replace the pricing grid with a usage-based savings calculator
decisions.action: Eliminate the plan grid from the default view. Replace with an interactive calculator: user inputs monthly transaction volume, system outputs a cost comparison and recommends one plan. Plan grid appears only as a secondary reference.
decisions.reasoning: Converts the pricing decision from a self-classification task into a calculation the user can't get wrong. This is a larger, riskier build than option A, but removes more of the measured complexity if it works.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires calculator engineering (5–8 days) and a defensible, current competitor-fee comparison — an inaccurate calculator would be worse than the current page. If enterprise contracts involve custom rates, those need a separate gated path.

decisions.label: Restructure the page to lead with ROI, bury the price
decisions.action: Reorder the page: savings calculator first (above the fold), plan selector second, CTA third. Show the modeled savings before revealing the subscription cost.
decisions.reasoning: Anchors value before cost, per published pricing-psychology research. Combines the risk profile of B with an additional information-ordering bet — untested on your specific audience.
decisions.tradeoff: Requires a full page restructure and copy rewrite, plus the same calculator-accuracy requirement as option B. The largest scope of the three options for an unverified incremental gain over B alone.
